newsitem.title: USA: Sun, union in talks over refinery job cuts.
newsitem.headline: Sun, union in talks over refinery job cuts.

text.p: Sun Co Inc and oil union leaders entered talks this week on proposed job cuts at the Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania refinery aimed at stemming the tide of red ink at the unprofitable plant.
Sun said early this month it would seek to cut more than 200 jobs or over 20 percent of the workforce, at the refinery as part of an overall plan to bolster profits.
A spokesman for the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers International union (OCAW) said moves to trim staff have been seen across the nation. Neither side elaborated on the talks.
The refinery, which has crude distillation capacity of 175,000 barrels per day (bpd), will see no reduction in that output from the proposed job cuts, the company said.

In another piece of its plan, Sun early this week also said it will cut 75 jobs in restructuring its Yabucoa, Puerto Rico refinery, begin refining residual fuel rather than crude, and phase out of fuels output in favor of lubricants.
The job cuts at Marcus Hook would come mostly from the 845 Sun employees at the refinery, though Sun also plans to cut some of the 50 contracted jobs at the Philadelphia-area plant.
"We did a benchmark study early in 1995 and found we were out of line with our competitors," said company spokeman Bud Davis. "It was pretty evident that we were not competitive."

The Marcus Hook refinery and Sun's Philadelphia complex, a two-refinery unit with total capacity output at 307,000 bpd, lost $44 million in the first nine months of 1996, Davis said, well above the $37 million lost in all of 1995.

"Generally in the industry we've seen these relentless types of cost cutting measures," said OCAW spokesman Rod Rogers. "And labor costs are one area that they can cut," he added, noting most other costs are fixed.
Though refining margins in the region have improved from the very poor levels seen earlier this year, company analysts agreed Sun badly needs take action at Marcus Hook refinery. "They
are one of the highest cost producers," said John Hervey, an analyst with Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette. "They're starting to feel the fire under their feet."
Hervey said the company had a strong need to renegotiate some of its labor contracts at Marcus Hook and to move to compete comfortably with refineries on the Gulf Coast.
"They have time to get this stuff done, but they have to get it done," he said.
Refining margins have moved higher, said Fedel Gheit, director of oil research at Fahnestock and Co., though he characterized the improvement as "from critical to guarded."
"Sun realizes that you cannot wait for the industry to improve," Gheit said.

Sun's Marcus Hook and Philadelphia refineries will also face increased competition in the summer of 1997 from the restart of the Tosco Trainer refinery in Marcus Hook, which was shuttered by British Petroleum Co Plc ahead of its sale to Tosco Corp in January.
"Tosco made a name for itself by buying units and then cutting costs. So Sun said, 'if they can do it, so can we,'" Gheit said.
